country.name: Ukraine
country.tagline: Swiss colonists at Shabo, Golitsyn's sparkling cellars in Crimea and a new generation of winemakers working through war.

stats.note: Before 2014 Ukraine had roughly 50,000 ha of vines including Crimea; occupation of Crimea removed about 17,000 ha and wineries providing about 60 percent of wine, and the war since 2022 has damaged or occupied more vineyards in Kherson, Mykolaiv and Zaporizhzhia. No current official total found.

country.overview:
Ukraine's southern coast has made wine since Greek colonists founded Olbia, Tyras and Chersonesus around the sixth and fifth centuries BC. The modern industry dates from the Russian Empire's conquest of the Black Sea steppe in the late eighteenth century. In 1822, with Alexander I's approval, winegrowers from the Swiss canton of Vaud founded the colony of Chabag, today Shabo, on the Dniester estuary in Bessarabia, and their descendants made wine there until the Second World War. Shabo is again Ukraine's largest wine company, with about 1,200 hectares and a wine culture centre on the old colony.

Crimea was the empire's showcase. Count Mikhail Vorontsov planted the south coast from the 1820s, the Magarach research institute was founded in 1828, and Prince Lev Golitsyn (1845 to 1915) built the sparkling wine cellars of Novy Svet (Noviy Svit), where his wine won at the 1900 Paris exhibition and was renamed for the coronation of Nicholas II, and directed the imperial Massandra winery (1894), whose collection of about a million bottles holds sherries and dessert wines back to 1775. Inkerman near Sevastopol ages wine in old limestone galleries. Crimea is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine; Russia has occupied and claimed it since 2014, and Massandra and other estates now operate under Russian control (the Russian-installed authorities 'nationalised' Massandra and sold it at auction in 2023).

The rest of Ukrainian wine is in the south (Odesa, Mykolaiv and Kherson oblasts) and in Transcarpathia (Zakarpattia) in the west, near Hungary, where Berehove and the Tisza valley have Tokaj-related traditions. Soviet Ukraine was the USSR's largest supplier of wine, with about 250,000 hectares before Gorbachev's 1985 campaign destroyed around 80,000. In the 2010s small producers such as Beykush (on the Berezan estuary near Mykolaiv), Kolonist and 46 Parallel in Odesa, Father and Sons, Chateau Chizay in Transcarpathia and Prince Trubetskoi's estate in Kherson started a quality movement, with local grapes such as Telti-Kuruk and Odessa Black alongside Saperavi, Riesling and Chardonnay.

Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 hit wine country hard. The Prince Trubetskoi estate at Kozatske in Kherson oblast was occupied, looted (including about 32,000 bottles) and its historic chateau destroyed; Artwinery, the sparkling-wine plant at Bakhmut with cellars in old gypsum mines, was forced out and moved production to Odesa; vineyards in Mykolaiv and Zaporizhzhia were mined and shelled. Producers kept harvesting, and exports to the EU have grown.

history.title: Greek colonies on the Black Sea
history.text: Olbia, Tyras (Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi) and Chersonesus made and traded wine; presses and amphorae survive at Chersonesus near Sevastopol.

history.title: The Swiss colony of Chabag
history.text: Vaudois winegrowers led by Louis-Vincent Tardent founded Chabag (Shabo) on the Dniester estuary; their wine was shown at the 1893 Chicago exposition.

history.title: Magarach Institute
history.text: The Russian Empire founded the Magarach viticulture research institute near Yalta; its collection holds thousands of vine varieties.

history.title: Golitsyn's Novy Svet
history.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn developed Novy Svet in Crimea into Russia's first great sparkling wine house and later directed Massandra (founded 1894).

history.title: Anti-alcohol campaign
history.text: About 80,000 ha of Soviet Ukraine's vineyards were destroyed under Gorbachev's campaign.

history.title: Occupation of Crimea
history.text: Russia occupied and annexed Crimea, an annexation not recognised by Ukraine or most of the world; Ukraine lost control of about 17,000 ha of vineyards and the Massandra, Novy Svet and Inkerman wineries.

history.title: Full-scale invasion
history.text: Kherson's Prince Trubetskoi winery was occupied, looted and its chateau destroyed; Bakhmut's Artwinery relocated; southern vineyards were damaged.

country.classification: Ukraine is building an EU-compatible system of protected geographical indications under its 2019 to 2023 legislation; historic names such as Shabo have been registered nationally. Most labels carry region and grape.
country.climate_soils: Continental steppe climate moderated by the Black Sea in the south, with hot dry summers and cold winters (vines are sometimes buried); chernozem and southern chernozem on loess. Transcarpathia is wetter and volcanic. Crimea's south coast is sub-Mediterranean, protected by the Crimean Mountains.

grapes.name: Telti-Kuruk
grapes.note: Aromatic local white of the Budjak (southern Bessarabia).

grapes.name: Odessa Black (Alibernet)
grapes.note: Soviet-era teinturier cross of Alicante Bouschet and Cabernet Sauvignon.

grapes.name: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon

regions.name: Odesa and Bessarabia
regions.tagline: Ukraine's main wine region, from Swiss Shabo to the Danube.
regions.summary: The Odesa oblast, including the southern Bessarabian Budjak between the Dniester and the Danube, holds the largest share of Ukraine's vineyards. Shabo, Kolonist, Frumushika-Nova, 46 Parallel and Tairove (home of the national viticulture institute) are here.
regions.history: Swiss Chabag (1822), Bulgarian and German colonies in the Budjak.
regions.terroir: Steppe chernozem near estuaries and the sea.
regions.grapes: Telti-Kuruk, Odessa Black, Aligoté, Rkatsiteli, Saperavi, Cabernet Sauvignon.

regions.name: Mykolaiv and Kherson
regions.tagline: Estuary vineyards now on the war's front line.
regions.summary: The southern oblasts around the Dnipro and Southern Bug estuaries, with Koblevo (a large Soviet-era winery on the Tylihul estuary), Beykush on the Berezan estuary and the Prince Trubetskoi estate on the Dnipro at Kozatske. Much of left-bank Kherson has been occupied since 2022.
regions.history: Prince Trubetskoi's estate dates from the late nineteenth century.
regions.terroir: Hot, dry steppe on sandy and chernozem soils by estuaries.

regions.name: Transcarpathia
regions.tagline: Volcanic hills on the Hungarian border.
regions.summary: Western Ukraine's Tisza valley around Berehove and Mukachevo shares volcanic soils and Hungarian traditions with nearby Tokaj; Chateau Chizay and family wineries grow Furmint, Traminer and local grapes.
regions.history: Part of Hungary until 1920, then Czechoslovakia, Hungary again and the USSR.

regions.name: Crimea
regions.tagline: Imperial cellars of Massandra and Novy Svet, under Russian occupation since 2014.
regions.summary: Crimea's south coast and valleys (Sudak, Alushta, Yalta, Balaklava, Sevastopol, Bakhchysarai) were the Russian Empire's luxury wine region. Internationally recognised as Ukraine, the peninsula has been occupied and annexed by Russia since 2014, and its wineries operate under Russian law; Russia treats 'Crimea' as one of its protected geographical indications.
regions.history: Greek Chersonesus; Vorontsov's estates (1820s); Magarach (1828); Golitsyn's Novy Svet and Massandra (1894).
regions.terroir: Sub-Mediterranean south coast under the Crimean Mountains; steppe in the north.
regions.grapes: Muscat, Kokur, Kefesiya, Ekim Kara, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Shabo wine culture centre
sites.text: The former Swiss colony of Chabag on the Dniester estuary, founded in 1822 by winegrowers from Vaud. Shabo, with about 1,200 hectares, is now Ukraine's largest wine company, with a museum of the colony.

sites.name: Massandra winery
sites.text: The imperial winery founded by Prince Lev Golitsyn in 1894 near Yalta, whose tunnel cellars hold about a million bottles, including dessert wines back to the eighteenth century. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Novy Svet sparkling wine cellars
sites.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn's estate near Sudak, where he dug cellars into the cliffs and made Russia's first great sparkling wine from the 1870s. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Inkerman winery
sites.text: Winery near Sevastopol that ages wine in limestone galleries left by quarrying. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Chersonesus
sites.text: The Greek city near Sevastopol (UNESCO), whose 'chora' of walled vineyard plots and wine presses is one of the best-preserved ancient agricultural landscapes anywhere.

sites.name: Koblevo
sites.text: A large winery on the Tylihul estuary between Odesa and Mykolaiv and one of Ukraine's best-known volume brands. Its vineyards sit on sandy chernozem by the estuary, where Black Sea air tempers the steppe heat.

sites.name: Chateau Chizay
sites.text: Winery near Berehove in Transcarpathia, on volcanic hills a few kilometres from the Hungarian border, part of a winegrowing area that shares soils and traditions with nearby Tokaj. It makes still and sparkling wines from Transcarpathian grapes.

sites.name: Prince Trubetskoi winery, Kozatske
sites.text: A historic estate on the Dnipro in Kherson oblast linked to Prince Trubetskoi, occupied in February 2022; its wine collection was looted and the chateau destroyed.

sites.name: Artwinery, Bakhmut
sites.text: Sparkling-wine plant founded in 1950 in former gypsum mines under Bakhmut; production moved to Odesa during the battle for the city.
